parts.title: Is a Spider an Insect? COUNT the Legs! (Part 1) | Animal Groups
parts.description:
An ant and a spider at the Singapore Botanic Gardens. Only one is an insect! Count the legs to find out. Part 1 of Primary 3 Science, Diversity: animal groups (insects, reptiles and mammals).

In this part:
• How to spot an insect: six legs, a pair of feelers, head, thorax and abdomen
• Wings are not the clue
• How to spot a reptile: dry, scaly skin (and Basil is one!)
• Be a scale on a monitor lizard's back: what cold-blooded means

Key words: insects; head, thorax, abdomen; reptiles; cold-blooded.
Watch Part 2: is a bat a bird?

TheOneApp, Explained: Singapore primary science, made fun. Play along with Pip, Basil and Momo: show fingers to lock in, keep score on your hand, beat the Buddies! Practise this topic in TheOneApp.

Singapore Primary 3 Science (2023 syllabus): Diversity, classification of living things: animals, insects, reptiles and mammals (Chapter 2, pp. 29–33; Let's Apply Q1–Q2, pp. 40–41). Also fits US NGSS 4-LS1-1 (Grade 3 to 4).
Try it at home: find a small animal on the way home. Look closely, but do not pick it up. Count its legs and tell someone at home. Wash your hands after.
Singapore and the US: fruit bats fly out at dusk near HDB blocks too. In the US (Grade 3), an alligator in Florida is a reptile, and a squirrel in the backyard is a mammal.

parts.title: Is a Bat a BIRD? How to Spot a Mammal (Part 2) | Animal Groups
parts.description:
It has wings and it flies at night in Palm Valley. Is a bat a bird? Part 2 of Primary 3 Science, Diversity: animal groups (insects, reptiles and mammals).

In this part:
• Be a hair on a fruit bat's back
• How to spot a mammal: hair or fur, milk for the young, warm-blooded
• Exam tip: same and different, with a reason
• Which one does not belong? The mystery creature
• Six animal groups, and the Exam corner

Key words: mammals, mammary glands, warm-blooded.
Watch Part 1 first! Next episode: fungi and bacteria.
